facts.fact: pH measures how acidic or basic (alkaline) water is.
The pH scale runs from 0.0 to 14.0; pure water is neutral at about pH 7.0, lower values are acidic and higher values are basic.
pH is logarithmic: each whole number is a tenfold change, so pH 4.0 is 10 times more acidic than pH 5.0 and 100 times more acidic than pH 6.0.
Some fish need a fairly specific pH while others tolerate a wide range; captive-bred fish usually need a specific pH less than wild-caught fish do.
Alkalinity (KH) is the water's buffering capacity, its ability to resist pH change; hard water buffers better than soft water.
Most freshwater tropical fish do best at pH 6.8 to 7.8.
Rift Lake cichlids prefer pH 8.0 to 9.0, while cardinal tetras (Paracheirodon axelrodi) from the Rio Negro live in water below pH 5.5.
Above pH 7.3 more of the ammonia is the toxic free form (NH3); below 7.3 more of it is the less harmful ammonium ion (NH4+).
High pH shifts ammonia toward its more toxic free form; pH matters more than temperature or salinity here.
Acidic water disturbs fish's ionic and osmotic balance, and nitrite and chlorine are more toxic at lower pH.
Low pH can release potentially toxic metals from sediments.
The biofilter is inhibited below pH 5.0; nitrifying reactions run fastest at about pH 8–9.
pH changes how medicines work: chloramine-T is more toxic in acidic water, so a lower dose is needed; organophosphates break down faster in alkaline water.
KH stabilises pH, feeds nitrifying bacteria and gives plants carbon; the target for most freshwater fish is 60–80 mg/L and for Rift Lake cichlids 120–200 mg/L.
KH acts as a buffer, so pH usually changes when KH changes.
At low pH (below 7), plants take up iron and other micronutrients more easily and ammonia becomes the much less toxic ammonium, but the beneficial bacteria colony is weaker.
At high pH (above 7), beneficial bacteria thrive and algae are easier to control, but micronutrients are less available to plants and CO2 dissolves less well.
Most aquatic plants do well at about pH 5.5 to 6.5; the page gives about 5 to 8 as a workable range for aquarium water and says no single pH suits every tank.
Bee shrimp (Caridina) prefer lower pH, unlike most tank animals, and the Tonina plant family does poorly at high pH.
The page gives the ideal pH for ornamental fish as about 6.5 to 7.5, depending on the species.
The page lists these pH ranges: goldfish (Carassius) 7.0–8.4, betta (Betta) 6.5–7.5, neon tetra (Paracheirodon) 5.0–7.0, discus (Symphysodon) 6.0–7.0, guppy (Poecilia) 7.0–8.0.
The page calls pH 5–8 the most ideal range for an aquarium.
Koi (Cyprinus) kept at pH 4.5 showed excess mucus, piping, flashing, fin twitching, poor appetite, listlessness, jumping, loss of buoyancy control and death.
Water is usually most acidic in the morning, because plants and algae use up CO2 by day and CO2 builds up overnight.
In planted tanks, pH rises by day through photosynthesis and falls at night as CO2 is released; the swings are bigger with low buffering or added CO2.

Old tank syndrome shows few, vague signs (more parasites and disease, occasional deaths or a sudden die-off) and only water tests confirm it: pH below 6.0, KH under 50 mg/L (often 0), high ammonia and nitrate.
Low pH is usually caused by poor tank hygiene and a build-up of organic matter.
As a tank ages, pH tends to fall gradually as organic waste builds up and mineral buffers are used up.
In old tank syndrome, the buffers are gradually used up, and once KH nears 0 the pH can swing sharply and crash.
Soft-water tanks are more prone to sudden pH drops (pH crashes) if they are not maintained correctly.
Things that raise pH include coral, limestone, snail shells, certain coloured gravels, some decorative rocks, high dissolved oxygen and baking soda.
Things that lower pH include peat moss, humic acid, CO2, acids (lemon juice, vinegar, vitamin C, strong mineral acids), Indian almond leaves (Terminalia catappa) and old filter media.

Coral releases calcium, magnesium and bicarbonate, raising pH, KH and gH; three-colour gravel mixed with small snail shells, 'cát muối tiêu' (crushed coral or ground shells) and white rocks such as 'đá tai mèo' do the same.
A filter that has not been cleaned for a long time can lower pH.
The page says source water (tap or well water), rocks, gravel and driftwood, and decomposing food and waste can all shift pH.
For old tank syndrome, do not do a full water change; change 10–15% of the water daily in week 1, the same amount every other day in week 2, then 20–25% twice a week in weeks 3–4, and retest.
The page notes that in old tank syndrome the low pH protects fish from the high nitrogen levels.
During ammonia poisoning, lowering pH to about 6.0–6.5 is recommended if the fish tolerate it, along with 25–50% water changes.
To raise low pH, do water changes, remove organic material and add sodium bicarbonate, limestone, crushed coral or shells.
To lower high pH, phosphate salts or acids such as sulfuric or nitric acid can be used, but phosphates should be avoided where possible because they feed algae; peat filtration is a natural option.
Baking soda (NaHCO3): dissolve 8–9 g in a glass of water and pour it in; the page says this raises pH by about 1 unit in 100 L and adds 25–50 TDS.
To lower pH with CO2, record the pH before CO2, then measure every 30 minutes and stop at about 1 unit below that baseline; the author calls a drop of 0.7 to 1 unit safe.

Acids such as nitric acid (HNO3) or phosphoric acid (H3PO4, used for discus tanks): dilute a few ml in a cup of water, pour it in, wait 5–10 minutes and retest; in the author's 300 L tank about 10 ml HNO3 lowered pH by 1 unit.
The author finds citric acid fine for ordinary shrimp, but advises care with high-value shrimp, and says vitamin C works but is weak.
Peat moss must be soaked or boiled until it releases no more tannin colour; it lowers pH slowly.
Dry Indian almond leaves (lá bàng, Terminalia) or their soaking water release mild natural acids; the page says they lower pH by 1–2 units.
Indian almond leaves (Terminalia) and blackwater lower pH only mildly and slowly.
Strong aeration removes CO2 and slightly raises pH.
Driftwood and Indian almond leaves (Terminalia) release organic acids from their tannins, which lowers pH.
Wood and driftwood should be soaked until they stop releasing colour, or they will tint the water.
Before adjusting high pH, find and remove what is raising it (coral, limestone, shells and similar) before adding anything to lower it.
If the materials raising pH stay in the tank, acid corrections wear off within a few hours to a day.
When setting up a tank, test your tap water first to check it suits the animals you plan to keep, and research each species' water needs before buying.
pH can be checked with test strips, liquid kits, pen meters or online monitors.
Litmus paper is cheap but less accurate and should be checked with another method; an electronic pH meter is more accurate but needs regular calibration and a clean probe.
Test pH at the same time of day each time and treat single readings with caution, because pH varies through the day.
Regular partial water changes remove pollutants and replace the minerals that buffer pH.
The page advises replacing about 20–30% of the water weekly with treated, tested water, testing pH weekly, keeping the filter clean and not overfeeding.
Old tank syndrome is prevented by regular water changes and filter cleaning.
Raise pH gradually, by no more than 0.5 units per day.
The page recommends changing pH by no more than 0.2 units per day.
Sudden or drastic pH changes can harm or even kill fish.
Change pH slowly to avoid shocking fish and plants.
Using coral to raise pH is a mistake because it also raises gH and TDS, which are hard to control.
Trying to match the native water of captive-bred fish is unnecessary; most are bred in different water, so acclimate them to yours.
Other mistakes are letting pH drift down in an old tank and not testing pH during cycling.
Any pH change must stay within each species' tolerance range.
Treat acids with care: do not breathe them in or touch them, and keep them away from children.
If the tank is stable, the author says not to worry much about the exact pH.
The author bought the acids he uses for pH (HNO3, H3PO4) at Kim Biên market (chợ Kim Biên) in Saigon; baking soda is cheap and sold at pharmacies.
Dragon stone ('đá da voi') and construction stone ('đá xây dựng') are said to raise pH.
Four-hole bricks ('gạch ống') used as substrate filler do not affect pH, river gravel ('sỏi suối') usually does not raise it, and white lava rock and tiger rock are fine.
A pH drop some time after adding fresh tap water may come from dissolved CO2 escaping; also check that the pH pen reads correctly.
If the source water is pH 8, acids may help; if it is below 8 but the tank is higher, something in the tank is raising pH and acid will not help.
Alum (phèn chua, KAl(SO4)2) does not lower pH, according to the Thuỷ sinh AZ author; its name refers to its sour taste.
